source_anchor: Sartre L'existentialisme est un humanisme (1946); L'Etre et le Neant Part I ch. II "La mauvaise foi" (1943); SEP "Jean-Paul Sartre" §2.3
instance: Sartre's claim that "existence precedes essence" combines with his analysis of bad faith (mauvaise foi) and radical freedom. State why bad faith is structurally different from a simple lie, and identify one concrete situation where someone uses it to evade the consequences of radical freedom.

answer_features.claim: bad faith is self-deception: the same consciousness is both deceiver and deceived
differs from a plain lie: a liar knows the truth and conceals from another; bad faith conceals from self
alt_phrasings: lie has audience bad faith does not
liar withholds from another bad faith withholds from self

answer_features.claim: concrete evasion: treating oneself as mere facticity (role / nature / past) to deny freedom (transcendence) — e.g., the waiter playing waiter, or "I had no choice"
alt_phrasings: plays a role to deny freedom
invokes nature or role to evade choice
denies the freedom to choose otherwise

candidate_responses.text: Bad faith is self-deception: the same consciousness is both deceiver and deceived, so unlike an ordinary lie there is no second party to whom the truth is concealed. A concrete case: the waiter who plays at being a waiter so completely that he treats his role as a fixed nature, evading the radical freedom that he must each moment choose to perform that role.
Sartre says we are condemned to be free, which is depressing.
It is a lie to oneself, where the deceiver and the deceived are the same. People often deploy it by saying "I had no choice", collapsing transcendence into facticity to evade freedom.
